opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a partnership where the human sets the direction and the professor agent handles a lot of the organizational heavy lifting. In the Virtual Lab, the human researcher typically comes in with the high-level goal. In our nanobody project, for example, the goal was to design new nanobodies that could bind to recent variants of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The human provides that framing, some of the key constraints, and the overall agenda for each meeting.

From there, the principal investigator agent, which is what we call the professor agent, has quite a bit of autonomy. It decides what kind of expertise the project needs and creates the scientist agents to fill those roles. In our case it created an immunologist, a machine learning specialist and a computational biologist, plus a scientific critic agent whose job is to poke holes in the ideas. The PI agent runs the team meetings, asks follow-up questions, synthesizes the discussion and makes the final calls on what the team should do next.

The human isn't micromanaging those conversations. In our experiments the human contributed only a very small fraction of the total words exchanged, maybe around one percent. The agents are doing most of the talking, debating and decision-making. But that small amount of human input is high leverage. It's like being a senior advisor to a lab. You don't sit in every discussion, but you check in at key decision points, redirect if things are going off track, and make sure the work stays grounded in what's actually feasible and meaningful.

I think that balance matters for a couple of reasons. One is that the agents can explore a lot of ideas and do the routine coordination very efficiently, often more broadly than a single human would. The other is that humans still bring judgment about which questions are worth asking, what resources are really available, and when something looks plausible on paper but doesn't make sense experimentally. And ultimately the wet lab validation, actually expressing the nanobodies and testing binding, is done by humans, so there's a natural checkpoint where reality comes back into the loop.

So I'd describe it as human-guided autonomy. The professor agent has real authority to organize and run the project, but within a scope the human defines and periodically reshapes. Over time, as these agents get more capable, I expect that ratio could shift further toward autonomy, but I think keeping the human in that steering role is important both for the quality of the science and for accountability.

r001.rationale: The response says the human researcher provides the high-level goal, key constraints, and meeting agenda, which guide the project.

r002.rationale: It says the professor agent decides what expertise the project needs and creates scientist agents to fill those roles.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way we designed the Virtual Lab, the human researcher really sits at the top, but with a pretty light touch. You come in with a high-level scientific agenda. In our case it was something like, "we want to design nanobodies that bind to the newer SARS-CoV-2 variants." That's basically the entire specification the human gives at the start.

Then the professor agent, which we call the principal investigator, takes over most of the organizational work. It decides what kind of team it needs. It literally proposes the agents it wants to hire, so an immunologist, a machine learning specialist, a computational biologist, and it writes their role descriptions. It sets the agenda for the team meetings, poses the questions, runs the discussion, and synthesizes the answers into decisions. Then it assigns the individual meetings where a single agent does a focused piece of work, like writing code for ESM or AlphaFold-Multimer.

So the autonomy is quite real. We were honestly a bit surprised at how much of the project management it could handle. But human guidance shows up in a few deliberate places. One is the initial framing of the problem, which matters a lot because that's what everything downstream is anchored to. Another is that we built in a scientific critic agent whose job is to push back and catch errors, which is a kind of institutionalized skepticism the human doesn't have to supply every time. And then the human steps in at a few checkpoints. We'd read the meeting transcripts and occasionally add a constraint, like "make sure the design actually fits what we can validate experimentally in the lab." Those nudges were short, maybe a sentence or two, but they had a big effect on the direction.

The analogy I like is that the human is less like a micromanager and more like a department chair or a funder. You set the goal, you check in periodically, you correct course if something looks off, but you don't tell the team how to run its meetings. And the payoff is that the human's time goes to the highest-leverage judgments, while the agents do the hundreds of pages of discussion and iteration that would take a real team weeks.

I'll say the one thing we're still learning is how much guidance is the right amount. Too little and the agents can drift into something elegant but impractical. Too much and you lose the reason you built the system. Finding that balance is really an empirical question, and I think it'll depend a lot on the scientific domain.

r001.rationale: The response says the human provides a high-level scientific agenda as the initial specification, while the professor agent handles most work downstream.

r002.rationale: It says the professor agent decides what kind of team it needs and proposes specialists, such as an immunologist and machine learning specialist, for the specified project.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a collaboration at different levels. The human provides the overall scientific direction: what problem we want to solve, what constraints matter, and what would constitute a useful result. Then the professor agent has autonomy to organize the work within that framework—identify the expertise needed, bring together the team, and coordinate the discussion.

That gives the human a way to guide the project without having to script every interaction. You can review what the team proposes, challenge an assumption, or redirect an experiment. The professor agent can then take that feedback and work through the next steps with the team. So autonomy and human guidance are complementary: the agent handles much of the coordination, while the human remains involved in shaping the scientific goals and judging whether the work makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response says humans set the overall scientific direction, including the problem, constraints, and useful result, while the agent organizes work within that framework.

r002.rationale: It says the professor agent identifies the expertise needed and brings together the team to pursue the human-directed project.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a collaboration at two different levels. The human provides the high-level scientific direction: What question do we want to answer? What constraints do we have? What would count as a useful result? Then the professor agent has autonomy in organizing the work around that goal—identifying the expertise needed, bringing together the scientist agents, and coordinating their discussions.

The human can also intervene along the way, give feedback, or redirect the project. So the autonomy is within a framework of human guidance. You don’t have to prescribe every interaction between the agents, but you still have opportunities to shape the research and evaluate whether it’s going in a productive direction.

r001.rationale: The response says the human sets the high-level scientific direction, including the question, constraints, and desired result, which are high-level project specifications.

r002.rationale: It says the professor agent organizes work around the human’s goal by identifying needed expertise and bringing together scientist agents.
